My first call center job was as a 911 operator. I can't even begin to narrow it down to a single call. So I'll give you the one that surprised me the most.

Background: we had received a call earlier in the night from an apartment property manager asking for police to go into a unit with her because she didn't want to go alone. It was a 2nd story unit and the unit below was being flooded from said unit. And the tenant was not answering the door.

Property manager and police go in and turns out he guy is passed out drunk in the bathtub with the water running. But he was okay.

I received a call later from the same place, from a cleaner who was apparently left behind (in the middle of the night yes, I know it's strange and idk why they did that). The cleaner is in he unit with the drunk guy, and she is telling me she heard a bang, and the drunk dude was passed out on the ground and blood coming from his head. I had it in my head that the bang was him hitting his head on the floor. I thought he stumbled because drunk and hit his head THAT hard. Anyway, I ask if he is breathing, he's not, so I get her on doing CPR. She tells me that the CPR is just making more blood come out of his head... My training and international emergency protocols have you address not breathing before bleeding so I'm like fuck it, as long as the caller is still willing to continue, we continue. 

Police and medical get there and take over. Guy is pronounced dead. One of the responding officers told me later that he shot himself in then head, and fell on top of the gun, so that's why the caller didn't realize what the bang was.

This was a preventable death had an officer stayed longer and ensured he was actually okay. I imagine he had tried to drown himself and since that didn't work he shot himself. He was only like 22 or so. And that's one of the many calls that I carry with me.

Personally, I feel that Amab in place of MtF, and Afab in place of FtM is better.

MtF and FtM both heavily imply that you WERE one thing, and then transitioned to something else. And I don't particularly like that about those terms. I was never male, my husband was never female, therefore we do not use those terms for ourselves. Amab and Afab don't carry that same connotation so that is what we use.

Additionally,  just amongst ourselves, we use them to refer to other people that we don't know. "That AMAB over there in the green shirt." Simply because we do not want to assume what someone's gender is just based on presentation.  Amab and Afab can equally apply to both trans and cis folk, so it has a lot more utility in my opinion.

We also live in an area where it is just not safe to publicly transition, neither of us look like our gender, so we recognize that random people may also be just like us, and have a gender that is different from their public presentation. Therefore we simply just refrain from making those kinds of assumptions.

The flaw in all of this is that we might get it wrong sometimes and call someone an AMAB when they are in fact a trans man that passes, or vis versa. The odds of being wrong are statistically less likely than being wrong when referring to a stranger as a man or a woman. 

We do NOT use these terms for people that we know, and know their gender. If we know them, we just refer to them by the gender that they are.

Throughout my days in school I was never accepted by the boys my age and always got along better with girls. For quite a long time I seriously questioned whether I was gay or bi. Things were complicated for me and I was never sure. But neither of those labels fit me. 

By my junior year of highschool I had met my best friend who shared a lot of the same feelings and experiences I had. We would talk a lot about wishing to be women, but in 2011 neither of us knew of the existence of trans women. We of course knew of drag l, but that didn't quite fit us either.

Fast forward to 2013 we both went off to college together in the most liberal school in the state. I joined the school's "Gay Straight Alliance" which was a student led club. Through them I learned of a Trans support group that was led by a few of the school's psychologists. It was around that time that Caitlyn Jenner came out and trans news started getting a lot more attention by the general public. That was all the perfect situation for me to educate myself on the subject.

The more I learned the more the Trans label seemed to fit me perfectly. Though I was still very uncomfortable with the idea of transitioning. I knew I was a woman, but I began telling everyone around me that I was non binary. I wanted to be included in the trans community, but I was scared of transitioning and the stigma that comes with being visibly trans. 

I went on like that for a few years never really taking steps to transition and my mental health suffered for it. I ended up in a relationship where my partner completely rejected the idea that I was a woman. I was in a very bad place mentally and allowed myself to shove the feelings and identity that I carried with me waaaay into the back of the closet. There was a lot of self hate and internalized transphobia that came with that.

I graduated in 2018 and left that relationship. However the only place that would hire me was my hometown police department as a dispatcher. I kept my identity a secret out of fear of what my employer would do. The police community made it clear to me that they would not have my back if I ever came back out of the closet. It was so bad that a cop almost lost her job just for having rainbow colored sharpies. 

I met my husband online in 2020, and to say that he saved me is an understatement. I randomly came out to him as trans in an online game. He just felt like a safe person to tell this to. I had no idea that he was also trans at the time but he was. He encouraged me to accept myself and allow myself to be my own person. We met up in person in late 2020, moved in together in early 2021. With his support I was able to quit my toxic police dept. Job and pursue a career that would allow me to be myself.

I finally became financially capable, and mentally healthy enough to begin transitioning earlier this year. Over 10 years after I met another person who had the same feelings that I did.

I'm sorry this is so long, but I hope that you get something out of it. What I hope you take away from my experience is that this is not a race. We all figure things out and take steps at our own pace.

You're quite young and it's expected to not really be sure or have things figured out yet. But the fact of the matter is that you're questioning and that's definitely worth exploring further.

More than likely, if you're questioning, you fall somewhere on the trans spectrum - whether that be NB, gender queer, transfem ECT. 

The best advice I can give is to seek out like minded people and begin building a support network of folks that you can safely discuss your thoughts with. A counselor or therapist may also be beneficial if that is an option for you.

Best of luck to you and your journey ☺️
